name: Function
quick: An assignment giving every allowed input exactly one output in the declared codomain.
definition: A function $f:A\to B$ has domain A and codomain B. Every a in A must have exactly one output f(a) in B. As a relation, it has exactly one pair starting at each allowed input.
example: The pairs (1,u), (2,u), (3,v) define a function from {1,2,3} to {u,v}.
confusion: Different inputs may share an output. One input having two different outputs is what violates the function definition.

name: Domain of a function
quick: The declared set of allowed inputs.
definition: For $f:A\to B$, the domain is A. A total function must supply an output for every member of A, so the domain is part of the specification.
example: $f(x)=1/x$ defines a real-valued function on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, but not on all reals.
confusion: A formula alone does not determine which inputs were intended.

name: Codomain
quick: The declared target set in which all outputs must lie.
definition: For $f:A\to B$, the codomain is B. It may contain targets never reached by the function. Surjectivity asks whether all of B is reached.
example: For $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ with $f(n)=2n$, the codomain is all integers but only even integers occur as outputs.
confusion: Codomain and image are different: the declaration and the actual reached outputs need not agree.

name: Total function
quick: A function defined at every input in its stated domain.
definition: Totality supplies an output for each declared input. The ordinary functions in this course are total unless explicitly stated otherwise.
example: The rule 1/x is total on the nonzero real numbers, even though it has no value at zero.
confusion: Total is relative to the stated domain; it does not mean defined at every conceivable object.

name: Partial function
quick: An assignment allowing some inputs in a stated input set to have no output.
definition: Where an output is defined it must still be unique, but some declared inputs may be left undefined. This is an explicit departure from the total-function convention used by default.
example: Division by x can be viewed as partial on all reals, with no value at zero, or total on the nonzero reals.
confusion: Allowing missing outputs does not allow multiple outputs for one input.

name: Image of a set under a function
quick: The outputs reached by the inputs in a specified set.
definition: For $S\subseteq A$, $f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\}$. The image of the whole domain, f(A), is also called the range in this course.
confusion: Repeated outputs contribute one set member, and the image need not be the entire codomain.

name: Preimage of a set
quick: All domain inputs whose outputs lie in the specified target set.
definition: For $T\subseteq B$, $f^{-1}(T)=\{x\in A:f(x)\in T\}$. This set is defined for every function, even when no inverse function exists.
example: For g(x)=x² on the reals, the preimage of {4} is {−2,2}; the preimage of {−1} is empty.
confusion: The preimage is a set of inputs. It does not claim that there is a unique input for each target.

name: Injective function
quick: A function that assigns distinct outputs to distinct inputs.
definition: Equivalently, f(x)=f(y) forces x=y for all domain elements. Also called one-to-one or an injection.
example: For f(n)=3n+2 on the integers, equality of outputs lets us subtract 2 and divide by 3 to obtain equal inputs.
confusion: Injectivity does not require every codomain element to be reached.

name: Collision of function inputs
quick: Two distinct inputs sharing the same output.
definition: A collision is a pair x≠y in the domain with f(x)=f(y). One such pair disproves injectivity.
example: The real square function has a collision at −1 and 1, both sent to 1.
confusion: One input with two outputs is not a collision of a function; it means the assignment is not a function at all.

name: Surjective function
quick: A function reaching every element of its declared codomain.
definition: For each b in B, some a in A must satisfy f(a)=b. Also called onto or a surjection.
example: The square function from the reals to the nonnegative reals is onto: target b is reached at √b.
confusion: A proposed preimage must lie in the actual domain. Solving an equation without checking the domain is insufficient.

name: Bijection
quick: A function that is both injective and surjective.
definition: Every codomain element has exactly one preimage. Therefore its assignment can be reversed to define a function on the entire codomain.
example: f(x)=3x+2 is a bijection from the reals to the reals, with inverse y↦(y−2)/3.
confusion: Bijectivity depends on the domain and codomain, not only the displayed rule.

name: Inverse function
quick: A function that reverses a bijection, undoing it in both directions.
definition: For a bijection $f:A\to B$, its inverse $f^{-1}:B\to A$ satisfies $f^{-1}(f(a))=a$ for a in A and $f(f^{-1}(b))=b$ for b in B.
example: The inverse of x↦3x+2 on the reals is y↦(y−2)/3.
confusion: The same superscript is used for preimages of sets, which exist without bijectivity. The argument and authored context determine the meaning.

name: Composition of functions
quick: Applying one function and then applying another to its output.
definition: With $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$, the composition $g\circ f$ sends a to g(f(a)). Apply the rightmost function first. Every intermediate output must lie in the next function’s domain.
example: If f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=x², then (g∘f)(x)=(x+1)², while (f∘g)(x)=x²+1.
confusion: Changing the order generally changes the function, even when both orders are defined.

name: Type of a function
quick: The stated domain and codomain of a function.
definition: The type $A\to B$ identifies allowed inputs and declared targets. Matching the inner codomain to the outer domain is a sufficient condition for composing functions.
example: If f maps real numbers to nonnegative reals, its outputs fit the real square-root function’s domain.
confusion: A matching algebraic expression is not enough when intermediate values fall outside the next domain.

name: Identity function
quick: The function that returns each input unchanged.
definition: For a set A, $\operatorname{id}_A:A\to A$ satisfies $\operatorname{id}_A(a)=a$. Composing with the appropriate identity changes no function value or type.
example: On {a,b,c}, its pairs are (a,a), (b,b), and (c,c).
confusion: The subscript specifies the set on which this identity acts.

name: Restriction of a function
quick: The same rule used on a subset of its original domain.
definition: For $S\subseteq A$, $f|_S:S\to B$ agrees with f at every input in S. It removes other inputs while retaining the codomain B.
example: Restricting the real square function to nonnegative inputs removes the collision between opposite numbers.
confusion: A domain restriction can lose surjectivity by removing the only input reaching a target.

name: Floor
quick: The greatest integer no larger than a given real number.
definition: $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is the unique integer k satisfying k≤x<k+1. It rounds downward, including for negative numbers.
confusion: Discarding the fractional part toward zero gives the wrong floor for negative nonintegers.

name: Ceiling
quick: The least integer no smaller than a given real number.
definition: $\lceil x\rceil$ is the unique integer k satisfying k−1<x≤k. It rounds upward, and leaves integers unchanged.
example: ⌈2.7⌉=3 and ⌈−2.7⌉=−2. Seven items in boxes holding three each need ⌈7/3⌉=3 boxes.
confusion: Ceiling is not rounding to the nearest integer; its direction is always upward.

name: Truncation toward zero
quick: Discarding the fractional part of a real number to move toward zero.
definition: For a positive input this agrees with floor; for a negative input it agrees with ceiling.
example: Truncating −2.7 gives −2, whereas floor gives −3.
confusion: Truncation and floor are different operations on negative nonintegers.

name: → — function domain to codomain
quick: Read f: A → B as “f maps the domain A to the codomain B.”
definition: A function $f:A\to B$ has domain A and codomain B. Every a in A must have exactly one output f(a) in B. As a relation, it has exactly one pair starting at each allowed input.
example: The pairs (1,u), (2,u), (3,v) define a function from {1,2,3} to {u,v}.
confusion: Different inputs may share an output. One input having two different outputs is what violates the function definition.

name: ↦ — maps an input to an output
quick: Read x ↦ x² as “x maps to x squared”; the two sides are an input and its output rule.
definition: The barred arrow $\mapsto$ describes a function rule by placing an input on the left and its assigned output on the right. Read $x\mapsto x^2$ as “x maps to x squared.” State the domain and codomain separately so that the rule can be checked at every allowed input.
example: The rule $x\mapsto 3x+2$ assigns 8 to input 2. Together with domain $\mathbb R$ and codomain $\mathbb R$, it specifies a real-valued function.
confusion: The arrow $A\to B$ declares input and output sets. The barred arrow $x\mapsto f(x)$ describes what happens to an individual input.

name: f(S) — image of a set
quick: The outputs reached by the inputs in a specified set.
definition: For $S\subseteq A$, $f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\}$. The image of the whole domain, f(A), is also called the range in this course.
confusion: Repeated outputs contribute one set member, and the image need not be the entire codomain.

name: f⁻¹(T) — preimage of a set
quick: All domain inputs whose outputs lie in the specified target set.
definition: For $T\subseteq B$, $f^{-1}(T)=\{x\in A:f(x)\in T\}$. This set is defined for every function, even when no inverse function exists.
example: For g(x)=x² on the reals, the preimage of {4} is {−2,2}; the preimage of {−1} is empty.
confusion: The preimage is a set of inputs. It does not claim that there is a unique input for each target.

name: f⁻¹ — inverse function
quick: A function that reverses a bijection, undoing it in both directions.
definition: For a bijection $f:A\to B$, its inverse $f^{-1}:B\to A$ satisfies $f^{-1}(f(a))=a$ for a in A and $f(f^{-1}(b))=b$ for b in B.
example: The inverse of x↦3x+2 on the reals is y↦(y−2)/3.
confusion: The same superscript is used for preimages of sets, which exist without bijectivity. The argument and authored context determine the meaning.

name: ∘ — function composition
quick: Applying one function and then applying another to its output.
definition: With $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$, the composition $g\circ f$ sends a to g(f(a)). Apply the rightmost function first. Every intermediate output must lie in the next function’s domain.
example: If f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=x², then (g∘f)(x)=(x+1)², while (f∘g)(x)=x²+1.
confusion: Changing the order generally changes the function, even when both orders are defined.

name: id — identity function
quick: The function that returns each input unchanged.
definition: For a set A, $\operatorname{id}_A:A\to A$ satisfies $\operatorname{id}_A(a)=a$. Composing with the appropriate identity changes no function value or type.
example: On {a,b,c}, its pairs are (a,a), (b,b), and (c,c).
confusion: The subscript specifies the set on which this identity acts.

name: f|ₛ — restriction
section: Restrictions, empty cases, and finite sizes
quick: The same rule used on a subset of its original domain.
definition: For $S\subseteq A$, $f|_S:S\to B$ agrees with f at every input in S. It removes other inputs while retaining the codomain B.
example: Restricting the real square function to nonnegative inputs removes the collision between opposite numbers.
confusion: A domain restriction can lose surjectivity by removing the only input reaching a target.

name: ⌊x⌋ — floor
quick: The greatest integer no larger than a given real number.
definition: $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is the unique integer k satisfying k≤x<k+1. It rounds downward, including for negative numbers.
confusion: Discarding the fractional part toward zero gives the wrong floor for negative nonintegers.

name: ⌈x⌉ — ceiling
quick: The least integer no smaller than a given real number.
definition: $\lceil x\rceil$ is the unique integer k satisfying k−1<x≤k. It rounds upward, and leaves integers unchanged.
example: ⌈2.7⌉=3 and ⌈−2.7⌉=−2. Seven items in boxes holding three each need ⌈7/3⌉=3 boxes.
confusion: Ceiling is not rounding to the nearest integer; its direction is always upward.

name: ℚ — rational numbers
quick: Numbers expressible as a ratio of two integers with nonzero denominator.
definition: The set $\mathbb Q$ consists of all numbers $a/b$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers and $b\ne0$. Different fractions can represent the same rational number. Every integer is rational because it equals itself divided by one.
example: The rule $f(n)=n/2$ sends integers to rational numbers. It therefore defines a function $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q$, although odd inputs prevent an integer codomain.
confusion: A decimal need not terminate to be rational: $1/3$ has a repeating decimal expansion. Irrational real numbers cannot be expressed as such a ratio.
